**Sūrat al-Fātiḥat al-Kitāb** (the Sura of the Opening of the Book), and it has seven verses.

*Al-fātiḥa* (the opening) originally means the first thing that is of the kind to be opened, like a book or a garment. It was applied to this sura because it is the means by which everything else is opened. Then it was applied to the first part of anything that proceeds in stages in some respect, such as speech that is gradually produced, and lines and pages that are gradually read or counted. The *tā'* (the ta marbūṭa) marks the transfer from the adjective to the noun. Alternatively, *fātiḥa* is a verbal noun meaning "opening," and it was applied to the sura by calling the thing acted upon by its verbal noun, to indicate its primacy, as though the sura were the opening itself. Its relation to the opening is direct, and the rest of the sura is related to it through the opening. This does not mean that the opening is an intermediary in the relation of the sura to the rest of it, so that the objection would arise that it cannot apply to the closing, since closing a thing means reaching its end, which only happens after contact with its first parts has ended. Rather, the meaning is that the opening related to the first part is an opening to it first and directly, and it is also, in the same way, an opening to the whole through it, because it is a part of the whole. The same applies to the closing. The arrival at the end of a thing first and directly befalls the last part, and the whole is reached through it in the manner that has been established. The "first" here includes the relative first, so there is no need to make the excuse that the name *fātiḥa* is applied to the noble sura in its entirety by reference to its first part.

*Al-Kitāb* here means the individual collection, not the common notion shared between it and its parts, as the scholars of legal theory (*ahl al-uṣūl*) use the term. There is no harm in the noble sura becoming known by this name in the early period of prophethood, before the collection was complete through the revelation of the whole, because the naming is from God, exalted is His name, or from the Messenger (ﷺ) with permission. It suffices for the naming that the collection is achieved in terms of its being realized in His knowledge, exalted and majestic is He, or in the Preserved Tablet, or in terms of its having been sent down all at once to the lowest heaven, and Gabriel dictated it to the scribes (*safara*), and then he would send it down to the Prophet (ﷺ) over about twenty-three years, as is well known. The genitive construction (*iḍāfa*) here has the sense of *lām* (of), as in "a part of the thing," not the sense of *min* (from), as in "a silver ring," because, as you know, the modified (*muḍāf*) is a part of the modified-to (*muḍāf ilayh*), not a particular instance of it. The basis of the naming is that the sura is the beginning of the Book in its known order, not its recitation in prayer, nor its teaching, nor its revelation, as has been said. As for the first, it is clear, since the meaning of *al-Kitāb* is not the common notion that applies to what is recited in prayer, such that its being the beginning would have to be considered in the naming. As for the last two, considering the beginning in terms of teaching or revelation would require observing the order in the rest of the parts of the Book from those two aspects, and there is no doubt that the order of teaching and the order of revelation are not in the pattern of the known order.

It is also called **Umm al-Qur'ān** (the Mother of the Qur'an), because it is the root and origin of it, either because it is its beginning, or because it includes the praise of God, exalted and majestic is He, the worship through His command and prohibition, and the explanation of His promise and threat. Or it is because of the totality of its meanings, from theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, which are the conduct of the straight path and the knowledge of the stations of the blessed and the abodes of the wretched. The meaning of *al-Qur'ān* is the same as the meaning of *al-Kitāb*. It is also called **Umm al-Kitāb** (the Mother of the Book), as the Preserved Tablet is also called by it, because it is the root of all created beings, and the clear verses that indicate their meanings, because they are clear and the ambiguous verses are referred back to them. The basis of the naming is what has been mentioned for Umm al-Qur'ān, not what Imam al-Bukhari reported in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*, that it is begun with in recitation in prayer, for that has no connection to the naming, as has been indicated.

It is called **Sūrat al-Kanz** (the Sura of the Treasure), because of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It was sent down from a treasure beneath the Throne." Or because of what is mentioned for Umm al-Qur'ān. It is also the reason for its being called *al-Asās* (the Foundation), *al-Kāfiya* (the Sufficient), and *al-Wāfiya* (the Complete). It is called **Sūrat al-Ḥamd** (the Sura of Praise), **al-Shukr** (Thanksgiving), **al-Du'ā'** (Supplication), and **Ta'līm al-Mas'ala** (Teaching the Request), because it includes them. It is called **Sūrat al-Ṣalāt** (the Sura of Prayer), because its recitation is obligatory in it. It is called **Sūrat al-Shifā'** (the Sura of Healing) and **al-Shāfiya** (the Healing), because of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is a healing from every illness." And **"al-Sab' al-Mathānī"** (the Seven Oft-Repeated), because it has seven verses that are repeated in prayer. Or because it was sent down twice, as is related: it was sent down once in Mecca when prayer was made obligatory, and again in Medina when the *qibla* was changed. It is definitively established that it is Meccan, because of the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:87]. It is Meccan by explicit text.

﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the basenmala at the beginnings of the noble suras. It has been said: it is not part of the Qur'an at all. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him), the position of Malik, the well-known position of the early Hanafis, and the view of the reciters of Medina, Basra, and Syria, and their jurists. It has been said: it is a singular verse of the Qur'an, sent down for separation and for blessing through it. This is the correct position of the Hanafis. It has been said: it is a complete verse from every sura that it begins. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and it has also been attributed to Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with both of them). The statement of Ibn al-Jawzi in *Zād al-Masīr* is to be understood in this sense, where he said: it was reported from Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) that it was sent down with every sura. This is also the position of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri, 'Ata', and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, and it is the view of the reciters of Mecca and Kufa and their jurists. It is the new opinion of al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him), and for this reason it is recited aloud according to him. So no weight is given to what has been reported from al-Jassas, that this view from al-Shafi'i was not preceded by anyone. It has been said: it is a verse of al-Fatiha, while being Qur'an in the other suras as well, without addressing whether it is a part of them or not, and without addressing whether it is a complete verse or not. This is one of the two views of al-Shafi'i according to what al-Qurtubi mentioned. It is reported from al-Khattabi that this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayra (may God be pleased with both of them). It has been said: it is a complete verse in al-Fatiha, and a part of a verse in the rest. It has been said: it is a part of a verse in al-Fatiha, and a complete verse in the rest. It has been said: it is a part of a verse in the whole. It has been said: it consists of verses of the Qur'an, numbering as many as the suras that begin with it, without being a part of them. This view is not attributed to anyone in the books. There is another view, mentioned by some later scholars without attributing it to anyone: it is a complete verse in al-Fatiha and is not Qur'an in the other suras. Were it not for considering it a complete verse, this would be one of the two possible readings of al-Shafi'i's ambiguity, for it has been reported from him that it is a part of a verse in al-Fatiha, while concerning the others his statement is ambiguous. It has been said: it is between being Qur'an or not. It has been said: it is between being a complete verse or not. Al-Imam al-Ghazali said: the sound position from al-Shafi'i is the second ambiguity. From Ahmad ibn Hanbal, concerning whether it is a complete verse and whether it is from al-Fatiha, there are two narrations, mentioned by Ibn al-Jawzi. It is also reported that he was with Malik and others who say it is not from the Qur'an. These are the well-known positions among these sayings, namely the first three. The consensus on its inclusion in the *maṣāḥif* (codices), together with the consensus that what lies between the two covers is the speech of God, exalted and majestic is He, requires the rejection of the first view, and the establishment of the common element between the last two, without any indication of the specificity of either one. For its being a part of the Qur'an does not require that it be a part of every sura of it, just as it does not require that it be a separate verse of it. As for what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with both of them), that whoever leaves it has left out one hundred and fourteen verses of the Book of God, exalted is He, and what is reported from Abu Hurayra that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Opening of the Book is seven verses, the first of which is *In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful*," and what is reported from Umm Salama that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the sura of al-Fatiha and counted *In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful* as a verse, and *Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds* as a verse," although each of them indicates the rejection of the second view, none of them is explicit in establishing the third view. As for the first, it indicates only that it consists of verses from the Book of God, exalted is He, numbering as many as the suras that begin with it, and not what is required, namely that it is a complete verse from each one of them, unless one resorts to saying that its being a verse numbering as many as the suras that begin with it, without being a part of them, is a view that no one has held. As for the second, it is silent on its status in the rest of the suras. As for the third, it speaks against it, while sharing with the second in the aforementioned silence.

The *bā'* in it is connected to an implied verb indicated by the verb with which the formula begins, just as it is in the naming of the traveler upon arriving and departing, and the naming of every doer upon beginning actions. Its meaning is seeking help, or association, for blessing, that is, "I read with the name of God," or "I recite." The fronting of the object is for emphasis and for the intention of restriction, as in *iyyāka na'budu* (You alone we worship). Supplying "I begin" (*abda'u*) is inappropriate, because it restricts the blessing to the beginning, which is contrary to what is intended, namely the blessing extending to the whole. The claim that supplying it fulfills the hadith in both wording and meaning, while supplying "I read" fulfills it in meaning only, is nothing, for the basis of compliance with the hadith is beginning with the naming, not supplying its verb. For the noble hadith does not say "every matter of importance," nor does it say "I begin" in it or imply it. This entire noble sura to its end is spoken on the tongues of the servants, as an instruction for them, and a guidance to the manner of seeking blessing through His name, exalted is He, and a guidance to the method of praise and asking for bounty. For this reason the noble sura is named for what is mentioned: the teaching of the request.

The *bā'* was given a kasra, though single letters should have a fatḥa, because it is specifically bound to being a particle of the genitive. Just as the *lām* of command and the *lām* of possession were given a kasra when they precede an explicit noun, to distinguish them from the *lām* of initiation. The word *ism* (name), according to the Basran grammarians, is among the nouns whose endings are dropped, whose initial parts are built on sukūn, and to which a *hamza* of initiation has been added, because their habit is to begin with the moving and stop on the still. This is supported by their conjugation of *asmā'*, *sammā*, *sammat*, and *suman*, which, like *hudan*, is a dialectal form of it. The poet said:

*"May God name you a blessed name, / May God prefer you with His preference."*

The metathesis is remote and not consistent. Its derivation is from *sumūw* (elevation), because it raises the named and gives it distinction. According to the Kufans it derives from *simma* (mark), and its origin is *wasm*, the *wāw* being dropped and the *hamza* of connection put in its place, so that its alteration would be reduced. This was objected to, on the ground that the *hamza* is not known to be prefixed to a word whose initial part has been dropped in their speech. Among their dialects are *simm* and *summ*. The poet said:

*"By the name of the One whose mark is in every sura."*

And he did not say "bi-Allah" alone, in order to distinguish it from the oath (yamin) and from seeking blessing (tayammun), or to make clear what is intended by seeking help (isti'ana) here. For it is sometimes directed to His Essence (exalted is He), and its reality is a request for aid in bringing about and producing the act, that is, "the outpouring of power" (ifadat al-qudra). The jurists of principles (usuliyyun, the scholars of legal theory) among our companions define it as that by which the servant is enabled to perform what is incumbent upon him. It is divided into "possible" (mumkina) and "facilitated" (muyassara), and it is the one requested by ﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help﴾. And sometimes it is directed to His Name, Mighty and Exalted, and its reality is a request for aid so that the act is valid in the sight of the Law (shar'an). For as long as it is not initiated with His Name (exalted is He), it is as if it did not exist. Since each of the two seekings of help is actual, it is necessary to specify the intended one by mentioning the Name. Otherwise, what is understood immediately from our saying "bi-Allah" when it is unqualified, especially when it is followed by the description ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, is the first seeking of help.

If it is said: then let the bā' (ba) be taken to mean blessing, and the mention of the Name may be dispensed with, since blessing can only be obtained through it. We reply: that is a consequence of the meaning of "Allah" being the Name, and is not the very point in dispute? So it is necessary to mention the Name, so that the possibility of the intended meaning being the Named Essence is cut off, and the bā' is then necessarily taken to mean the second seeking of help, or blessing.

The alif was not written because of the frequency of its use. They said: the bā' was lengthened as a substitute for it.

As for "Allah": its origin is "al-Ilah" (the God). Its hamza was deleted contrary to analogy, as indicated by the obligation of assimilation (idgham) and the substitution of the alif and lam for it, since they are obligatory with it and it has been stripped of the meaning of definiteness. For this reason it is said "Ya Allahu" with the hamza of the alif-lam retained (qat'), since the analogically deleted element is treated as present, and so it does not need to be compensated by what has been mentioned of assimilation and substitution. It was also said: it follows the analogy of lightening the hamza, so that assimilation and substitution are among the special features of the Glorious Name, by which it is distinguished from all others, just as its Named Essence is distinguished from all others by the attributes of perfection that are not found in anything else.

"Ilah" originally is a generic noun (ism jins), applied to every object of worship, whether rightly or wrongly, that is, regardless of the attribute of being true or false, and not considering either of them specifically. Then it became predominant for the object of worship in truth, as with "al-najm" (the star) and "al-su'q" (the thunderbolt). As for "Allah" with the hamza deleted, it is a proper name (alam) specific to the object of worship in truth, and it is never applied at all to anyone else.

Its derivation is from "al-ilaha", "al-ulaha" and "al-uluhiyya", meaning worship, as the lexicographer al-Jawhari explicitly states. It is a noun derived from these meaning "the one worshipped" (al-ma'luh), like "al-kitab" meaning "the written" (al-maktub), and not an attributive adjective derived from them. The proof is that it is described, but is not itself used as a description, as one says "an ilah wahid" (one God), but one does not say "shay'un ilah" (a thing is a god), just as one says "kitabun marqum" (an inscribed book) but does not say "shay'un kitab" (a thing is a book). The difference between the two is that what is designated by an attributive adjective is an undetermined essence, considered in terms of its being characterized by a specific meaning subsisting in it; so its signified is composed of an undetermined essence, with no particularity considered alongside it at all, and of a specific meaning subsisting in it. The key point of the matter is that particularity, so whatever essence that meaning subsists in, the application of the attribute to it is valid, as is the case with verbs, and for this reason it works as its verb does, like the active and passive participles. But what is designated by the aforementioned noun is a determined essence together with a specific meaning, so its signified is composed of those two meanings without the meaning having precedence over the essence, as is the case with the attributive adjective. For this reason it does not function as the attributive adjective does.

It was also said: it is derived from "alaha", meaning "to be bewildered", because the intellects and understandings are bewildered regarding His affair, exalted is He. As for "alaha", like "abada" in form and meaning, it is derived from "al-ilah", which is derived from "ilh" with a kasra. Likewise "ta'alaha" and "ista'laha", in the manner of "istanwaqa" (a she-camel becoming like a she-camel in its ways) and "istahjara" (a stone-like formation), from "al-naqa" (the she-camel) and "al-hajar" (the stone).

It was also said: it is from "alaha ila fulan", meaning "he found peace with him", because hearts are tranquil in remembering Him, exalted is He, and souls are at rest in knowing Him. It was also said: it is from "alaha" when one is alarmed by a matter that has befallen him, and "alahahu ghayruhu" when someone else gives him protection, since the one who seeks refuge in Him, exalted is He, takes refuge in Him, and He protects him in reality or in his own supposition.

It was also said: its origin is "lah", as a verbal noun from "laha, yaliyu", meaning "to be concealed and exalted", and it was applied to the agent for emphasis.

It was also said: it is a proper name for the Glorious Essence from the outset, and upon this rests the matter of Divine Unity in our saying: "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah). It is not hidden that the exclusivity of the Glorious Name to His Essence, exalted is He, such that it is not possible to apply it to anyone else at all, is sufficient for this. And it does not detract from this that this exclusivity came about by way of predominance, after it was originally a generic noun.

It was also said: it is an attributive adjective in origin, but because it became predominant for Him, such that it is not applied to anyone else at all, it became like a proper name. This is refuted by the impossibility of using it as a description.

Know that what is meant by the indefinite in the phrase of Divine Unity is the object of worship in truth. So its meaning is: there is no individual of the objects of worship in truth except that object of worship in truth.

It was also said: its origin is "Laha", in Syriac, which was then arabized by deleting the second alif, adding the alif and lam to it, and emphasizing its lam when the preceding letter is not kasra, as a sunna; and it was said: in every case. Deleting its alif is a grammatical error, by which the prayer is invalidated, and by which an explicit oath is not concluded. It has come in poetry out of poetic necessity, in the verse:

Oh, may Allah not bless Suhayl,
since Allah has blessed no men.

And ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ are two attributes formed from "rahima" (to have mercy), after it was made intransitive like the natural dispositions, by transferring it to "rahuma" with a damma, as is well known. It has been said that "al-Rahim" is not an attributive adjective of the resembling type (sifa mushabbaha), but rather an intensive form (sigha mubalagha), as stated explicitly by Sibawayh in the phrase "huwa rahimun fulanan" (he is merciful to so-and-so).

Mercy (al-rahma) in language is tenderness of heart and compassion (al-in'itaf), and from it comes "al-rahim" (the womb), because of its tenderness toward what is within it. What is meant here is bestowal of grace and beneficence, and both are intended by way of applying the name of the cause, in relation to us, to its distant or near effect. For the Names of Allah (exalted is He) are taken in view of their ends, which are actions, and not their beginnings, which are affections.

The first of these is among the predominant attributes, since it is not applied to anyone else, exalted is He. Its being prevented from taking nunation (sarf) is only because it was assimilated to the most common pattern in its category, without regard to the specific attribute that has come upon it. For just as the form "fa'la" is forbidden to exist, so is the form "fa'lana", and so considering it would require combining both the nunation and its absence, so it is necessary to return to the original of this word before its particularization, by comparing it to its counterparts of the pattern "fa'ala yaf'alu". If all of them are prevented from nunation, because the form "fa'la" is established in them, it is known that this word too, in its origin, is one in which the form "fa'la" is established, and so it is prevented from nunation. And in it there is more emphasis than in "al-Rahim". For this reason it is said: "O Most Merciful of this world and the Hereafter" and "O Especially Merciful of this world."

Its being placed first, although the analogy would be to place it second, is in observance of the style of ascending to the higher; as in the saying: "So-and-so is a learned, outstanding scholar; a brave, valiant hero; and a generous, overflowing benefactor." For, by its exclusivity to Him, Mighty and Majestic, it has become worthy of being paired with the Glorious Name specific to Him, exalted is He. And because what indicates the great blessings, their magnitudes and their roots is more deserving of precedence than what indicates their subtleties and branches. The mention of the two noble attributes separately is to stir the chain of mercy.

﴿Al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn﴾.

﴿Al-ḥamdu lillāh﴾: *al-ḥamd* (praise) is describing someone with a beautiful quality on account of a beautiful quality, whether that quality is voluntary or is the source of the act, in a manner that conveys its being directed toward the one praised. By this aspect *ḥamd* is distinguished from *madḥ* (commendation), which lacks it. What indicates this is the difference you observe between them in how they take their object, in your saying *ḥamidtuhu* and *madaḥtuhu*. The second (*madaḥa*) takes its object in the manner in which most verbs take their objects. The first (*ḥamida*), however, takes its object in a way that indicates the sense of *inhāʾ* (reaching to or conveying to), as in your saying *kallamtuhu* (I spoke to him), which is expressed by the *lām* of communication in your saying "*qultu lahu*" (I said to him). Similar are *shakartuhu* (I thanked him), *ʿabadtuhu* (I worshipped him), and *khadamtuhu* (I served him), since the connection of each of these indicates the aforementioned meaning. The reality of the matter is that the object of every verb is in fact the event proceeding from its agent, and no difference at all can be conceived in how any verb connects to it. As for the object in which the action is located and takes place, since its connection to it and its falling upon it occur in various ways, according to what the particular characteristics of the verbs require in accordance with their different meanings, some verbs require that it be affected by it with complete affectation that has an effect on it, like most verbs, while others require that it be affected by the least affectation, either by reaching to it, like *iʿāna* (assisting) for example, or by beginning from it, like *istiʿāna* (seeking help) for example. For each mode of its connection to the object, a manner suitable to that mode is taken into account, distinct from what is taken into account in the last two modes. Thus the first kind of connection is classed among the connection to the real (direct) object, in consideration of the strength of the affectation. Each of the last two kinds is made to be a connection by means of the appropriate preposition. Your saying *aʿantuhu* (I helped him) indicates that the assistance reaches to him, and your saying *istaʿantuhu* (I sought his help) indicates that it begins from him. It may also be that a single verb has two objects, connecting to one of them in the first manner and to the other in the second or third manner, as in your saying *ḥaddathanī l-ḥadīth* (he related the hadith to me) and *sa'alanī l-māl* (he asked me for the wealth). The relating, though a single verb, connects to you in the second manner and to the hadith in the first. Likewise the asking is a single verb which connects to you in the third manner and to the wealth in the first. There is no doubt that the difference between these three manners, their divergence, and the particularity of each of the mentioned objects with what is attributed to it of them, is something about which no doubt or objection can be conceived, although it does not become fully clear except in translation and explanation. The basis of this difference is nothing other than the difference of the verb or the difference of the object. Since there is no difference in the object of *ḥamd* and *madḥ*, it is established that their difference lies in the manner of connection, owing to their definite difference in meaning. That said, it has been said: *madḥ* is unrestricted from the condition of choice; it is said, "I praised Zayd for his beauty and the slenderness of his figure." In any case, there is no synonymy between them, but rather a kinship by way of *al-ishtiqāq al-kabīr* (major derivation, i.e., shared root-letters with transposition or similarity of meaning), and complete correspondence in meaning, like *al-naṣr* (victory) and *al-taʾyīd* (support). These two correspond in meaning without being synonyms, because of the difference you observe between them in how they connect to the object. The synonym of *al-naṣr* is only *al-iʿāna* (assistance), and the synonym of *al-taʾyīd* is *al-taqwiya* (strengthening). So reflect on this. Then, what has been mentioned as the explanation is the well-known meaning of *ḥamd* and the one suited to the context of exaltation. As for what is mentioned in the books of lexicography regarding the meaning of *riḍā* (contentment) in an unrestricted sense, as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ and in their saying, "This matter has a praiseworthy outcome," and in the saying of the physicians, "a praiseworthy crisis" (*buḥrān maḥmūd*), it is not restricted to the agent, let alone to choice. Thus it is far removed from deserving the will here, whether independently or by implication, by taking *ḥamd* to include both meanings, since there is no valuable benefit in affirming it for Him, Mighty and Majestic.

As for *shukr* (gratitude), it is the response to a blessing with praise, with the courtesies of the limbs, and with the heart's firm conviction in describing the Benefactor with the attribute of perfection, as the one who said:

*"Blessings have brought you three things from me: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart."*

Thus *shukr* is more general than *ḥamd* in one respect and more specific in another. Its opposite is *kufrān* (ingratitude). Since *ḥamd* is among the branches of *shukr*, it is included in the spreading of the blessing and in acknowledging its importance, and it points more clearly to its place, because of the concealment in the work of the heart and the possibility of error in the actions of the limbs. Hence *ḥamd* was made the head of *shukr* and its foundation in His saying (ﷺ): "*Al-ḥamdu raʾsu sh-shukr; mā shakara llāha ʿabdun lam yaḥmadhu*" ("Praise is the head of gratitude; no servant thanks God who does not praise Him").

Its being in the nominative is by way of the inchoative (*mubtadaʾ*), and its predicate is the adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf*). Its original form is the accusative, as is the case with verbal nouns (*maṣādir*) governed by their implied verbs, which are hardly ever used together with them, such as *shukran* (thanks) and *ʿajaban* (how amazing!). It is as if it were said, "We praise God with praise," with the *nūn* of narration, so that it agrees with what is in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, because the agent is one in all of them.

As for what has been said, that it is an explanation of their praise of Him (Exalted), as if it were said, "How do you praise?" and it was answered, "You alone we worship," this is, despite the fact that there is no need for it, something without validity in itself. The supposed question must be one that the coherence of the speech requires and that minds and understandings are led to. There is no doubt that the one praising, after he has offered his praise to Him (Exalted) in that suitable manner, does not occur to anyone to ask about its manner. Moreover, the supposed question does not correspond to the answer, since it is directed toward specifying the one worshipped, not toward explaining the worship, so that it could be imagined that it is an explanation of the manner of their praise. The excuse that the meaning is "We single You out for worship, and through this the manner of praise becomes clear" is an inversion of the matter and a contrivance to reconcile the established revealed text with a supposed assumed (question).

After (all) the "this and that" (*al-latayya wa-llatī*), if the question were assumed to come from the side of Him, Mighty and Majestic, then the subtle point of *iltifāt* (shift of address) would arise, on which both the early and later scholars agreed. But if it were assumed to come from the side of another, the order would be disrupted, because the answer would then be built upon addressing Him (Exalted).

With this, the corruption of what has been said, that it is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnāf*) answering a question which the enumeration of these great attributes applied to the One described by them would require, is made clear. It is as if it were said, "What is your relation to Him? And how is your turning toward Him?" and then it was answered by restricting worship and seeking help to Him. For ignoring the side of the questioner completely, and building the answer upon addressing Him, Mighty and Exalted, is something that the sanctity of the revelation must be held free from.

The truth from which there is no escape is that it is a resumptive clause issued by the praiser purely out of consideration of His (Exalted) being described by the mentioned sublime attributes, which necessitate full turning toward Him, without anything else intervening there, as you will be made aware in detail. The choice of the nominative over the accusative, which is the original, is to indicate that the establishment of praise for Him (Exalted) is due to His essence, not due to the establishment of any establisher, and that this is a constant, continuing matter, not a newly renewed occurrence, as the reading in the accusative indicates. This is the secret of why the greeting of Abraham, the Friend (*al-Khalīl*), to the angels, upon them be the greeting and peace, was better than their greeting to him, in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace."﴾

Its definiteness is for the genus (*lil-jins*), and its meaning is an indication of the reality as it is present in the mind of the hearer. The intended meaning is the restriction of the reality of praise to Him (Exalted), which calls for restricting all its individual instances to Him, Glorified be He, by way of demonstrative argument. However, this is not based on the premise that the actions of servants are created by Him (Exalted), so that the individual instances corresponding to the good actions proceeding from them would return to Him (Exalted). Rather, it is based on placing those individual instances and their motivations, in the rhetorical context, in the position of non-existence in quality and quantity.

It has been said: it is for *al-istighrāq* (comprehensive inclusion), which arises from intending the reality insofar as it is realized within all its individual instances, according to what the context requires.

It is also read: ﴿al-ḥamdu lillāhi﴾ with a *kasra* on the *dāl*, in harmony with the following *lām*, and with a *ḍamma* on the *lām*, in harmony with the preceding *dāl*, on the basis of treating the two words, because they are so often used together, as one word, like *al-Mughīra* and *munḥadar al-jabal* (the slope of the mountain).

﴿رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾: It is read in the genitive (*bi-l-jarr*), making it an attribute (*sifa*) of God. Its *idafa* (construction) is genuine (*haqiqiyya*), and it conveys definiteness (*ta'rif*) in every case. This necessarily determines that the sense is one of continuity. It was also read in the accusative (*mansub*) by way of praise (*al-madh*), or as governed by what the preceding sentence implies, as if it were said: "We praise God, the Lord of the worlds." It cannot be governed by "al-hamd" (praise), because the verbal noun with the definite article (*al-masdar al-muhallā bi-l-lām*) rarely governs, and because that would require separating the governing word from the governed by the predicate (*al-khabar*).

"Al-Rabb" (the Lord) is originally a verbal noun (*masdar*) meaning upbringing (*al-tarbiya*), which is bringing a thing to its perfection gradually, step by step. It is applied to the agent as an intensive form (*mubalagha*), like "al-adl" (the just). It has also been said that it is an attributive adjective (*sifa mushabbaha*) from "rabbahu yarubbuhu," like "nammahu yanummuhu," after making it intransitive by transferring it to the pattern "fa'ula" with a *damma*, as is well known. It was applied to the owner (*al-malik*), because he guards what he owns and raises it. It is not applied to anyone other than God (exalted is He) except when qualified, as in "rabb al-dar" (the master of the house) and "rabb al-dabba" (the owner of the beast). Among its uses is His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So he will give his lord wine to drink﴾, and His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Return to your lord﴾. As for what is in the two *Sahihs*, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let none of you say: Feed your lord; give water to your lord; and let none of you say: My lord; let him say: My master and my protector," it has been said that the prohibition therein is for reverence (*li-l-tanzih*). As for the plural *arbab*, since its application to God (glorified is He) is not used, its application admits both unqualified and qualified use, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Are scattered lords better...﴾, and so on.

"Al-Alam" (the world) is a name for that by which the Creator is known (*ma yu'lamu bihi*), like "al-khatam" (the seal) and "al-qalib" (the mold). It has become specifically dominant for the created things by which the Creator (exalted is He) is known, that is, in the common measure shared between their species and their totality. Just as it is applied to each species among them, as in the expressions "the world of the spheres," "the world of the elements," "the world of plants," "the world of animals," and so on, it is also applied to the whole collectively, as in our saying: "The world with all its parts is originated."

It has also been said that it is a name for the rational beings of the angels and the two weighty creatures (humans and jinn), and that its inclusion of what is other than them is by way of subordination (*al-istitba'*). It has also been said that by it only humans are meant, since each one of them, by virtue of containing counterparts of what is in the greater world of substances and accidents, is known through them to the Creator, just as he is known through the world that is in him as a separate world. For this reason he was commanded to contemplate the self as well as the horizons, so it was said: ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾. The first view is the most correct and manifest.

The choice of the plural form serves to show that His lordship (exalted is He) encompasses all the species, and the definite article serves to comprehend all the individuals of each of them entirely. For if it were singular, it might be supposed that the intended meaning of the definite article is the reality (*al-haqiqa*) as such, or the comprehensiveness of the individuals of a single species in the manner indicated in the definition of praise (*al-hamd*). Since this is valid with the help of the definite article, "al-alam" (the world), even though it is not applied to the individual referents of its meaning, is treated as the plural (*manzila al-jam'*). So much so that it has been said: it is a plural that has no singular from its own form. Just as the definite plural comprehends all the individuals of its singular even if it does not apply to them, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾, that is, every good-doer, so too "al-alam" includes the individuals of the species named by it, even if it is not applied to them, as though they were individuals of its notional singular. From the requirement of this treatment is treating its plural as the plural of a plural. Just as "al-aqawil" (sayings) comprises each of the individual sayings, the word "al-alamin" comprises each of the individual species, which cannot be counted.

It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he said: "God (exalted is He) has eighteen thousand worlds, and this world is one of them."

It was pluralized with the *waw* and *nun* ending, even though that is specific to the attributes of rational beings and what is equivalent to them among proper names, because it indicates the meaning of a proper name, together with considering the dominance of rational beings over others.

Know that the non-application of the name "world" to each one of those individuals is only by way of dominance and convention. As for its original basis, there is no doubt about the validity of the application, definitively, for the realization of the referent is certain. For just as God (glorified is He) is inferred from the totality of what is other than Him, and from each species of its species, so He (exalted is He) is inferred from each part of that totality, and from each individual of those species, because the need for the Influencer who is necessary of existence in Himself is realized in the whole. For everything that has appeared in the appearances, whether lofty or humble, and has presented itself in these presences, whatever it may be, is a clear proof of the Skilful Creator, and a plain path to the world of monotheism.

As for the comprehensiveness of His lordship (mighty and majestic is He) over all, it needs no explanation. For nothing that the circle of possibility and existence encompasses, whether celestial or terrestrial, abstract or material, spiritual or corporeal, but in its very essence is such that, were the effects of nurture to be cut off from it for a single instant, it would not find stability nor would the abode be at peace with it, except in the pit of nonexistence and the abysses of ruin. Rather, from the most holy Presence (exalted is His majesty, and sanctified is He in every time that passes and every moment that elapses) there is poured upon it the varieties of overflowing bounties connected to His essence, His existence, His attributes, and His perfections, which the sphere of expression cannot encompass and which none knows except the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. This is necessary: just as nothing of the possible things deserves existence in itself from the beginning, so it does not deserve it in continuance. Rather, that comes from the presence of the First Origin (mighty and exalted is He). Just as its existence cannot be conceived from the beginning unless all modes of its original nonexistence are closed to it, so its persistence in existence after its realization by its cause cannot be conceived unless all modes of its accidental nonexistence are closed to it, because permanence is one of the properties of necessary existence. It is evident that what its existence depends upon, of the existential matters that are its causes and conditions, even if finite (since what enters existence must be finite), nonetheless the negative matters that have a role in its existence, which are expressed as the removal of impediments, are not like that. For there is no impossibility in one thing having impediments without limit, on whose removal its existence or persistence depends, that is, their remaining in nonexistence, while their existence in themselves remains possible. So the maintenance of those impediments, which are unlimited, in nonexistence is a nurturing of that thing in unlimited respects.

In sum: the effects of His nurture (mighty and majestic is He), overflowing upon each individual of the existents, at every moment of existence, are unlimited. So glory be to Him, glory be to Him! How great is His dominion! The eyes do not perceive it with their glances, nor do the intellects apprehend it with their thoughts. His affair cannot be matched, and His beneficence cannot be exhausted. We are bewildered in knowing Him, and falling short in performing the rites of His thanks. We ask You, O God, for guidance to the ways of knowing You, and success in discharging the rights of Your blessing. We cannot count the praise due to You. There is no god but You. We seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 1, verse 3:

﴿الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾: These are two attributes of Allah. If by the mercy contained in them is meant that which is specific to the rational beings among the worlds, or the bounties that overflow upon all after they have come out into the stage of existence, then the reason for placing them after the attribute of Lordship (rububiyyah) is clear. If, however, what is meant is that which encompasses all things in all their stages, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾, then the reason for the order is that nurturing (tarbiyah) does not necessarily entail being accompanied by mercy. Mentioning the two attributes after it serves to indicate that He (Exalted is He) is bountiful in it, acting by virtue of His preceding mercy, without any obligation upon Him, and that it occurs in the best possible manner. Limiting the description of Him (Exalted is He) to these two in the basmalah is because this is more fitting to the state of one who seeks blessing and seeks help through His glorious name, and more in accord with its purposes.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 1, verse 4:**

﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾: This is the fourth attribute of Him (exalted is He). Its being placed after the first attributes is something whose reason needs no explanation. The people of the two sacred sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah) read "Malik" (King), from *al-mulk* (sovereignty), which is an expression for overpowering authority, dominant control, complete victory, and the ability to exercise total disposition over the affairs of the people through command and prohibition. This reading is the most suitable to the context of its being joined to "the Day of Judgement," as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿To whom belongs the dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾. It has also been read as "Malk" with a light pronunciation, as "Malaka" in the past tense, as "Malika" in the accusative for praise or as a circumstantial clause, and in the nominative, either with tanwin (unmodified) or as an annexed construction, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject. It has also been read as "Maliku" annexed, in the nominative and accusative.

"Al-yawm" (the day) in common usage is an expression for the period of time between sunrise and sunset. In the sharia (religious law) terminology, it is the period between the second dawn (*al-fajr al-thani*) and sunset. The intended meaning here is the unrestricted time.

"Al-din" means recompense, whether good or bad. From it is the second usage in the well-known proverb: "As you do, so shall it be done to you" (*kama tadin tudan*). The first usage is in the verse of the Hamasah:

*"Nothing remained but the enemies, whom we repaid as they had repaid us."*

As for the first usage in the first case, and the second usage in the second case, these are not recompense in the literal sense. It is only so named by way of *mushakalah* (association of terms), or by naming a thing by the name of its cause, just as the intention of standing and recitation was named by their names in His saying, mighty is His name: ﴿When you stand up to prayer﴾, and His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾. Perhaps this is the secret behind forming the *mufa'alah* (the form denoting mutual action) from verbs whose causes subsist in their objects, such as "I punished the thief" (*'aqabtu al-lis*) and its like. For the act of theft, which is the cause of punishment, falling upon the thief, was treated as if it were the standing of the one who causes it, namely the punishment. So it is as if it subsisted on both sides and proceeded from both of them. Thus the *mufa'alah* form, which indicates sharing between two parties, was constructed.

The annexation of "the day" to it (the Day of Judgement) is for the slightest connection, like the annexation of all temporal adverbs to the events that occur in them, as in "the day of the Confederates" (*yawm al-ahzab*) and "the year of the Conquest" (*'am al-fath*). Its being specified from among all that occurs in it, such as the resurrection, the gathering, and the reckoning, is because it is more effective in encouragement and warning, for what has been mentioned of the resurrection and other things are the beginnings and preliminaries of recompense.

The annexation of "Malik" to "the day" is an annexation of the active participle to an adverb of time, in the manner of extended usage based on treating it as if it were an object, while the meaning remains as it is, like their saying: "O thief of the night, (you are) the people of the house," meaning: "Master of all the affairs of the worlds on the Day of Judgement." The absence from its annexation of the definiteness that would justify its being a qualifier of a definite noun is only the case when it is intended for the present or the future. But when the intention is the continuous, established state, as is most fitting to the context, there is no doubt that it is a true annexation (*idafah haqiqiyyah*), like the annexation of the *sifah mushabbahah* (attribute resembling the active participle) to something other than its object, in the reading "Maliki yawm al-din." And "the Day of Judgement," although it is not continuous in all times, nevertheless, because its occurrence is certain and its permanence is everlasting, is treated as the certain and continuous. It is also permissible that it be intended as the past on this understanding, as the reading in the past tense testifies.

What has been mentioned about treating the adverb as if it were the object is only in terms of meaning, not in terms of grammatical inflection (*i'rab*), so that it would not follow that the annexation is merely verbal (*lafziyyah*). Do you not see that you say of "Malik 'abdihi ams" (the master of his slave yesterday) that it is annexed to the object, in the sense that it is so in meaning, and not that it is in the accusative position in its place?

The specification of it by the annexation is either for its magnification and its awe, or to show His exclusive (exalted is He) control of the affairs in it. The severing of the figurative connections between "*al-malak*" (the owner) and "*al-amlak*" (the owners) at that point entirely, and the attribution of those glorious attributes to Him (glory be to Him), is a justification for what preceded of the specification of praise to Him (exalted is He), which entails the specification of the deserving of it to Him (exalted is He), and a preparation for what follows of restricting worship and seeking help to Him. For each one of them expresses the necessity of the establishment of each one of them for Him (exalted is He), and the impossibility of its establishment for other than Him. As for the first and the fourth, it is clear, because they explicitly address His being Lord and Master, and that everything else is what is nurtured and owned by Him (exalted is He). As for the second and the third, His (exalted is He) being described by them is only in relation to what else exists among the worlds, and that requires that all be those upon whom He bestows favour. Thus it becomes clear that each of those attributes, just as it indicates the necessity of the establishment of the matters mentioned for Him (exalted is He), indicates the impossibility of their establishment for anything other than Him absolutely. This is what is meant by *al-ikhtisas* (exclusivity).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 1, verse 5:

﴿It is You we worship, and it is You we ask for help﴾: an *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person, from the third person to the second person); a variation of the discourse from one style to another, in keeping with the path of eloquence, in the diversity of speech and the course of excellence, as the context requires, because moving from one style to another is more effective in attracting souls and winning hearts. It occurs from each of the speaker, the addressee and the absent party to each of the other two, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾; the verse; and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them﴾; and other shifts found in the Revelation, for secrets that call for them and virtues that demand them. Among the fine insights this noble station singles out is that the restriction of worship and seeking help to Him, Exalted is He, is due to the sublime attributes ascribed to Him, which necessitate for Him, Exalted is He, the most perfect distinction and the most complete manifestation, such that the obscurity of the third person gives way to the clarity of direct presence. Thus the use of the form of address is called for, and it signals that the right of the reciter, after he has reflected on what has preceded, namely His being singled out, Exalted is He, in His most holy Essence, which makes Him worthy of worship; His being distinguished in His Essence from all else entirely; His independence in sublime attributes and the rulings of lordship that set Him apart from all the individuals of the worlds; and the dependence of all upon Him in essence and existence, at the beginning and in continuance, according to the detail to which allusion has passed, is that he should ascend from the rank of proof to the level of direct witnessing, and move from the world of the absent to the landmarks of witnessing, and observe himself within the precincts of holiness, present in the assemblies of intimacy, as if he stands before his Lord, inclined before Him, supplicating with humility and submission, and knocking with humble entreaty at the door of intimate conversation, saying: "O You, whose are these affairs of Essence and attributes, we single You out for worship and for help, for every other thing, whatever it may be, is far from deserving existence, let alone deserving to be worshipped or to be asked for help." Perhaps this is the secret behind the noble surah being specially required to be recited in every rak'ah of the prayer, which is the servant's intimate conversation with his Lord, and a sign of wholly devoting oneself to Him.

"Iyya" is a detached pronoun in the accusative case. What is attached to it of the *kaf*, *ya'* and *ha'* are particles added to specify address, speech or the absent party; they have no place in *i'rab* (grammatical case-analysis), like the *ta'* in "anta" and the *kaf* in "ara'aytaka". As for what al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) claimed of its being a genitive construction, citing as evidence what he related from some Arabs: "When a man reaches sixty, then (beware of) him and the young men," it is not something to be relied upon. It was also said: the pronouns are themselves, and "iyya" is a support for them to make them detached. It was also said: the pronoun is the whole combination. It has been read as "iyyaka" with a light pronunciation and with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda, and as "hiyyaka" with the hamza changed to a ha'. Worship (*'ibadah*) is the furthest extent of humbling oneself and submission, and from it comes "a paved path" (*tariq mu'abbad*), meaning a levelled one; servitude (*'ubudiyyah*) is less than it. It was said: worship is doing what Allah is pleased with, and servitude is contentment with what Allah, Exalted is He, has done. Seeking help (*isti'anah*) is asking for assistance in the manner whose explanation has already passed. The fronting of the object in both cases is for the restriction and specification mentioned, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is Me that you should fear﴾, together with what it contains of exalting and giving importance to it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: its meaning is: "We worship You and worship no one other than You."

The repetition of the accusative pronoun is to make explicit the restriction to Him, Exalted is He, of each of worship and seeking help, and to display the delight in intimate conversation and address. The worship is mentioned first because it is among the requirements of the meaning of the glorious Name, though the attributes applied to it support it too. As for seeking help, it is among the rulings based on the attributes mentioned; and because worship is a right of Allah, Exalted is He, while seeking help is a right of the one who seeks it; and because worship is obligatory absolutely, while seeking help follows what is sought in terms of being obligatory or not. It was also said: because mentioning the means before the object asked is more conducive to being answered and accepted. This is on the basis that the application of seeking help is to the object sought, so as to include every thing sought, as they said. It has also been said: since what is asked is help in worship and enabling the proper performance of its rites as they should be, which is fitting to the status of the Revelation and suitable to the state of the one praising, for his seeking help is preceded by considering one of His acts, so that he seeks Him, Exalted is He, to bring it about. It is clear that when he is absorbed in considering His affairs, Exalted is He, and occupied with performing what that consideration requires of praise and glorification, it hardly occurs to his mind, of His acts and states, except full turning towards Him and complete directing of oneself to Him. Indeed He has done this by singling out worship for Him, Exalted is He, first, and by asking for guidance to what leads to Him at the end. How, then, can it be imagined that he occupies himself between these two with what does not concern him of the affairs of his worldly life, or with what encompasses it and other things? It is as if it were said: "And it is You we ask for help in that, for we are unable to fulfil His rights without help from You." Then the order is clear, and in it there is an indication of the loftiness of the rank of worship of Allah, Exalted is He, the difficulty of attaining it, that it is for the worshipper the noblest of aims and goals, that it is among His gifts, Exalted is He, and not among the deeds of the self; and there is a fitness with what follows it of supplication that is not hidden. It was also said: the *waw* is for the state, meaning: "It is You we worship while seeking help from You." The choice of the form of the first person plural in both verbs is to signal the weakness of one's self, its unfitness to stand alone in the stations of greatness, and to present worship and ask for help and guidance independently; and that this can only be conceived from a group of which one is a part, and an assembly of which one is among the company, as is the custom of kings; or to signal that all monotheists share with him in the state that befalls him, based on the convergence of the proofs that compel this. It was also read "nista'in" with a kasra on the nun, according to the dialect of the Banu Tamim.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 1, verse 6:

﴿Guide us to the straight path.﴾ This is a specification of the most important kinds of the help that is asked for, and a designation of what is most important, or an explanation of it, as if it were said: "How should I help you?" And it was said: "Guide us." Guidance (hidayah) is indicating with gentleness what leads to the desired goal, and for this reason it is restricted to good. His (exalted) saying: ﴿So guide them to the path of the Blazing Fire﴾ is used in the manner of mockery. The original construction is that it takes "ila" (to) and "li" (for). As in His (exalted) saying: ﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?" Say: "God guides to the truth."﴾ It is therefore treated like "ikhtara" (to choose) in His (exalted) saying: ﴿And Musa chose his people﴾. Upon this is His (exalted) saying: ﴿Surely We shall guide them to Our ways.﴾

God's guidance (exalted is He), although it divides into kinds that can hardly be counted, is confined to ordered genera. Among them are the inward (anfusiyyah), such as the bestowal of the natural and animal faculties by which a person's natural and animal actions proceed from him, and the perceptive faculties and the outward and inward senses by which he is enabled to establish his worldly and otherworldly interests. Among them are the outward (afaqiyyah), which are either creational (takwiniyyah), expressing the truth through the tongue of the state, namely the placing of the proofs deposited in each individual of the world, as has been hinted at earlier; or revealed (tanziliyyah), making clear the details of the theoretical and practical rulings through the tongue of speech, by sending the Messengers (ﷺ) and sending down the books that contain the various kinds of guidance, of which is guidance to the path of reasoning by those creational outward and inward proofs, and drawing attention to their places. As is indicated in summary in His (exalted) saying: ﴿And in the earth are signs for those who have certainty﴾ ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾ And in His saying, (glorified and exalted): ﴿Surely in the alternation of night and day, and in what God created in the heavens and the earth, are signs for a people who are mindful.﴾ Among them is the special guidance, which is the unveiling of secrets upon the heart of the one guided, by revelation or by inspiration. Each of these levels has a person who aims for it and a seeker who asks for it. What is sought is either its increase, as in His (exalted) saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾; or steadfastness upon it, as is narrated from Ali and Ubayy (may God be pleased with both of them): "Guide us" means "make us firm."

The word guidance in the latter sense is definitively figurative (majaz). As for the first sense, if the concept of increase is considered as entering into the meaning used, it is also figurative; and if it is considered as outside of it, indicated by the contextual indicators, it is literal (haqiqah), because additional guidance is guidance, just as additional worship is worship. So there is no combining of the literal and the figurative.

It is read "arshidna" (guide us to right conduct). "Al-sirat" means the highway. Its origin is with sin, changed to sad because of the presence of ta, like "musaytir" in "musaytir" (overseer), from "sarta al-shay'" when one swallows it. It was named thus because it swallows up the travelers when they take it, just as it was named "laqm" because it gulps them down. The sad may also be pronounced with the sound of zay, seeking closeness to the original letter from which it was changed. All of these have been read, but the most eloquent of them is the pure sad, and this is the dialect of Quraysh, and it is the one established in the Imam (the standard text). Its plural is "suruṭ," like "kitab" and "kutub." It is like "al-tariq" (the road) and "al-sabil" (the way) in masculine and feminine usage. "Al-mustaqim" means the straight, and what is meant by it is the path of truth, which is the upright, tolerant religion (al-millah al-hanifiyyah al-samhah) that is moderate between excess and deficiency.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 1, verse 7:

﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾: a substitute for the first term, a substitute of the whole (badal al-kull). It is in the position of repeating the governing verb, inasmuch as it is the intended object of the reference. Its purpose is emphasis and specification, namely to state explicitly that the path of those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, who are the Muslims, is the sign of uprightness and the one attested to as being straight, such that when the straight path is mentioned, the mind goes to none other than it. The unrestricted mention of favour is intended to be comprehensive, for the blessing of Islam is the emblem of all blessings, so whoever attains it has gained them all in their entirety. It has been said that the intended meaning is the prophets (peace be upon them). Yet the more apparent view is that they are those mentioned in His words, mighty is He: ﴿Those are with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous﴾, as attested by what precedes it in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path﴾. It has also been said that they are the companions of Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them both) before the abrogation (naskh) and distortion (tahrif). It has been read as "the path of those whom You have favoured". Bestowal (in'am) means the conveyance of a blessing (ni'mah). Originally, a blessing is the state in which a person finds pleasure, namely softness (al-lin). Then it was applied to what the soul finds pleasant of the good things of this world. The blessings of Allah, exalted is He, despite their being impossible to count, are essentially confined to two kinds: worldly and otherworldly. The first has two divisions: that which is bestowed (wahbi) and that which is acquired (kasbi). The bestowed also has two divisions: spiritual, such as the breathing of the spirit into him and his being equipped with reason and the perceptive faculties that follow it, for these, although they belong to the category of guidance, are sublime blessings in themselves; and bodily, such as the formation of the body, the faculties inherent in it, and the conditions accompanying it, namely health and the soundness of the limbs. The acquired is the purification of the soul from vices and its adornment with noble morals and excellent qualities, the adornment of the body with natural good conditions and pleasing ornaments, and the attainment of status and wealth. The second (otherworldly) is the forgiveness of what has been committed of error, His good pleasure with him, and his being settled in the highest of the 'Illiyyin with those brought near. The desired one is the last division, and what serves as a means to attaining it is from the first division. O Allah, grant us that by Your great bounty and Your vast mercy.

﴿other than those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray﴾: an attribute of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), on the basis that it is an expression for one of the mentioned groups, famous for being favoured and for uprightness of path. Necessarily, this fame entails their being distinguished from those described by the word "other than" (ghayr) as joined to it, namely those characterised by the two opposite attributes just mentioned, I mean absolutely those who have incurred anger and those who are astray. Thereby it acquired a definiteness that validates its being used as an attribute of a definite noun, as in your saying: "Upon you is movement other than stillness." They were described thus to complete what precedes it and to signal that safety from what those (others) were afflicted with is in itself a great blessing, that is, those who combined the unrestricted blessing, which is the blessing of faith, with the blessing of safety from anger and error. It has also been said that the intended meaning of the relative pronoun is a group of believers, not specific individuals; thus it carries the sense of an indefinite noun, like the definite article when it is intended as a generic within some individuals rather than a specific one. This is called the "mental definite" (al-ma'hud al-dhihni). By "those who have incurred anger" and "those who are astray" are meant the Jews and the Christians, as occurs in the Musnad of Ahmad and the Tirmidhi. Thus the word "other than" remains in its generality, indefinite, like its described noun. You know well that making the relative pronoun an expression for an indeterminate group mentioned as mentioned breaks the substitute relationship of what is added to it with what precedes, for the basis of the matter is that the path of the believers is the sign of uprightness, attested to be straight in the manner you have realised earlier. It is clear that this is by virtue of its being attributed to and ascribed to all of them, not to some vague part of them. By this it becomes clear that there is no way to make "other than those who have incurred anger" a substitute for the relative pronoun, because you know that the nature of a substitute is to give its governing term additional emphasis and confirmation, and an added clarification and explanation. There is no doubt that the most that can be achieved in our case is that it acquires, from what is attached to it, a kind of definiteness that validates its being an attribute of the relative pronoun. As for it deserving to be the intended object of the reference, conveying the benefits mentioned, that is not so. It has been read in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (hal), the governing verb being "You have favoured"; or on the basis of praise; or on the basis of exception, if blessing is interpreted as encompassing both categories. Anger is the agitation of the soul for the purpose of retribution. When it is ascribed to Allah, glory be to Him, what is meant is its end, by way of applying the name of the cause in relation to us to its nearer effect, if what is meant is the intention of retribution, or to its more remote effect, if what is meant is retribution itself. It is permissible to take the statement as a figure of speech, by likening the state abstracted from His wrath, exalted is He, towards the disobedient, and the intention to take retribution on them for their disobedience, to what is abstracted from the state of a king when he becomes angry with those who disobeyed him and intends to take revenge on them and punish them. "Upon them" (alayhim) is in the nominative case, dependent on "those who have incurred" (al-maghdub), standing in place of its subject. Turning away from ascribing anger to Him, exalted is He, as with bestowal, follows the path of the revealed courtesies in attributing blessings and goods to Him, mighty and majestic is He, rather than their opposites, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿He who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ ﴿And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾; and His words, exalted is He: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾. The "la" (not) is superfluous, to emphasise the sense of negation conveyed by "other than", as if it were said: "neither those who have incurred anger nor those who are astray." For this reason it is permissible to say "I am not one who hits Zayd", on the analogy of "I Zayd not hitter", though "I Zayd like a hitter" is not permissible. Error (dalal) is deviation from the straight path. It has been read: "and other than those who are astray", and it has been read: "and not those who are astray (al-da'alin)", with the hamza, according to the dialect of one who was eager to flee from the meeting of two quiescent letters.

﴿Amin﴾: a verb-noun (ism fi'l) meaning "answer" (istajib). "Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the meaning of 'amin', and he said: 'Do'." It is built on the fatha like "ayna" (where), owing to the meeting of two quiescent letters. It has two dialects: lengthening its alif and shortening it. He said:

... And may Allah have mercy on a servant who says "amin"

And he said:

... "Amin", so Allah increased the distance between us

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Gabriel taught me 'amin' when I finished reciting the Opening of the Book, and said: 'It is like the seal upon the Book'." It is agreed that it is not part of the Qur'an, but it is recommended to conclude the noble surah with it. The well-known view of Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) is that the one praying should say it silently. It is also reported from him that the imam should not say it, because he is the one who supplicates. Al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him) said the same. Abdullah ibn Mughaffal and Anas ibn Malik transmitted the silent recitation from the Prophet (ﷺ). According to al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him), it is said aloud, on the basis of what Wa'il ibn Hujr narrated: "That the Prophet (ﷺ), when he recited 'and not those who are astray', said 'amin' and raised his voice with it." "From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: 'Shall I not inform you of a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel or the Qur'an?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'The Opening of the Book; it is the seven oft-repeated and the great Qur'an which I have been given'." And from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, when a people has incurred from Allah a decreed and inevitable punishment, a child from among their children reads in the Book 'Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds', and Allah, exalted is He, hears it, and so He lifts the punishment from them for forty years."
